body: Eleven days after a shoulder operation, and told twice not to lift anything, a joiner of fifty-six is sitting in his front room at half past nine on a Saturday morning with his tea going cold beside him and the radio off, because his wife has gone to her sister’s and the house is his for six hours. By twenty to ten he has worked out how to sort the screws on the dining table one-handed, into the lids of jam jars, by length. He would not describe himself as restless. He would say he was tidying up.

That is what obedience to a rest order looks like in a competent man. He was not defying anybody. He simply could not locate the thing he was supposed to be doing instead, because there is nothing to do instead, and that is the whole difficulty.
Be still, and know that I am God. It is usually filed at the gentle end of Scripture, printed over a photograph of a lake at dawn, and it is in fact the hardest instruction in the book.

Harder than the ethical ones, and it is worth being exact about why. Forgive, give, tell the truth when it costs you, go and be reconciled before you bring your gift — those are genuinely difficult, and every one of them shares an enormous advantage, which is that an action exists. Something can be done, today, badly, and the doing counts as obedience. A man can forgive his brother through gritted teeth and have obeyed. Be still offers nothing of the kind. There is no motion that constitutes compliance, no first move, nothing to make a start on, and for anybody whose life has been solved by making a start, that is not a small problem.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air today. Two of the numbers, HM 366.20 and HM 365.40, are assigned to Shalom: Be Still and to Stillwater. Both are in build, not yet on air, still silent.

Holding numbers for stillness is a peculiar commitment, because a station of that kind can never demonstrate that it worked. There is no engagement to point at, and the better it does its job the less anybody does anything at all. It is held anyway, because the command is in the book and the book does not grade it optional. Every other command can be obeyed by doing something. This one is disobeyed by doing anything, and a dial that only knows how to fill an hour has nothing to offer the one hour that is not meant to be filled.

The modern treatment is to convert the thing into a technique with an outcome. Rest becomes recovery, stillness becomes focus, sabbath becomes a way of protecting next week’s output, and the whole business is quietly re-shelved under performance. It is not cynicism that does this. It is that there is no other category available. A culture that can only value what produces something will eventually explain the one practice that produces nothing in terms of what it produces, and will destroy it politely, while recommending it warmly.

The Hebrew is no help to anybody hoping the command is softer than it looks. The word is harpu, from a root meaning to let drop, to slacken, to release a grip — nearer to release than to quiet. And the setting is not a retreat centre: it is nations in uproar and mountains carried into the middle of the sea. The stillness is commanded inside the emergency rather than after somebody has dealt with it, which is why nearly every tradition that takes it seriously ends up building an external structure for it — a fixed hour, a set form, a length decided in advance by somebody who is not you.
Left to themselves people do not become still. They become busy in a quieter way, and call it rest because it involves sitting down.

The usual answer is willpower dressed as discipline: the personal quiet time, the resolution to be better about it, the plan starting Monday. It deserves a fair hearing, because for some people it plainly works and there is no virtue in sneering at a man who gets up at six to read his Bible. But it hands the length of the thing to the person doing it, and a person who cannot stop is the worst available judge of when he has stopped for long enough. He will decide, at four minutes, that he has got the general idea. Then he will go and look at the gutter. The faculty being relied on is the faculty that is broken.
You cannot use effort to stop making an effort.

A woman of thirty-nine is parked outside a primary school at ten past three, twenty minutes early, because being early is the only way she can be certain of not being late. Ordinarily she uses the twenty minutes: the shopping list, the message she has been meaning to send, the thing at work she has been carrying since Thursday. Today the radio is still on because it was on when she turned the engine off, and somebody is singing something she cannot follow, in a language she has never learned, and there is nothing in it she can act on. So she watches the gate. When the children come out she has decided nothing and achieved nothing, and getting out of the car she notices that her jaw is not clenched.
She did not become still. She was, for twenty minutes, unable to make any use of what was playing, and from the inside that turned out to be the same thing.

Twenty minutes with an unclenched jaw is not the presence of God, and calling it that is the sort of inflation that makes sensible people give up on the subject. It cuts the other way as well, and this should be said plainly: for a good number of people stillness is not restful. It is when the thoughts arrive. Take away the noise and what floods the room is the thing the noise was for, and a scheduled hour of quiet is no kindness to somebody in that position.

But look at what the woman in the car actually had, because it was not quiet. It was something audible she could not use. Silence gives the mind the whole floor; a song in a language you do not speak occupies the ear and offers the hands nothing, which is an entirely different arrangement. The grip releases because there is nothing there to grip. That cannot be practised and is not a technique, which is the point of it — the one faculty a person like that cannot deploy is the faculty that got them into it.

So the reason this is the hardest instruction is not that stillness is unpleasant. It is that the ordinary machinery of obedience — decide, begin, apply yourself, review — is exactly what has to be switched off, and there is no version of switching it off that does not use it. Which leaves external things: a form, a fixed length, an hour that runs whether or not anybody is in the mood. Crude, and with a considerably better record than good intentions.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing, so here is the part that is not.

The band carries four kinds of programming. There is music, which is most of it. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on with children in the room. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. A quiet block of numbers is set aside for sleep and rest — Shalom: Be Still, Stillwater, Inspire Lullaby — and all of those are assigned and in build, not yet on air. Which leaves the fourth kind, and it turns out to be the useful one here.

Go to HM 329.00 — Israel Inspire, hosted in Hebrew. The recommendation is not sentimental about the language of the psalm, although it is that language. It is practical. Almost nobody reading this will follow a word of it, and that is the entire reason to put it on. Music with English words in it is something you can work: evaluate the theology, disagree with a line, decide the singer is straining, catch yourself composing what you would say about it afterwards. Every one of those is a grip. In Hebrew there is nothing to take hold of. The ear is occupied and the hands are given nothing, and a man sorting screws by length will find, after a while, that there is no reason to be sorting them.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So do not set aside an hour, and do not resolve anything, because resolutions are for commands that have actions in them. Put HM 329.00 on this afternoon while you are somewhere you cannot do very much — a parked car, a waiting room, a front room with your arm in a sling — and let it play in a language you do not have. You will not be able to tell whether it is working. That is not a fault in the arrangement. It is the first honest sign that you have let go of something.
